Golden Ratio in an Irregular Pentagon

AreaAlgebra
Game: Bend a lopsided five-sided shape in which the five triangles at its corners always stay the same size, and see what else stays true.
How to play: Drag the three big dots, X, Z and D, and watch the pentagon and the numbers below change. Tick the boxes to show the corner triangles and the letters.

Look for the math

Only one thing is asked of the pentagon: the five triangles ABC, BCD, CDE, DEA and EAB all have the same area. Everything else follows, however crooked the pentagon is.

Diagonals parallel to sides

Triangles ABC and ABE have the same area and the same base AB, so C and E are at the same height above AB: the diagonal CE is parallel to AB. The same argument works for every diagonal and the side it leaves out. The test builds 200,000 random pentagons with the applet's construction and finds all five parallelisms every time.

The golden ratio and the area

Let the diagonals BD and CE meet at M. Then ABME is a parallelogram. Call the area of BCM x, with the corner triangles of area 1. Because BCDE is a trapezoid, DEM also has area x, and comparing ratios of areas gives x / (1 - x) = 1 / x, that is x² + x - 1 = 0, so x = (√5 - 1)/2. Then BM/DM is the golden ratio and the pentagon has area 3 + x = (5 + √5)/2 = 3.618... times one corner triangle. The numbers above the picture show these values for the pentagon you made.

More of the same

These pentagons are exactly the stretched and sheared copies (affine images) of a regular pentagon, which explains why nothing but the shape changes. The pentagon the diagonals make inside is of the same kind, with area 1/φ4 of the outer one; extending the sides into a star gives five points that form another one, φ4 times as big. The test confirms both on every random pentagon.

Drag X until the pentagon is as long and thin as you can make it. Is the ratio of its area to a corner triangle still 3.618?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
